pos: adv. (affirmative and intensive; rendering Hebrew 'aph, gam, and ken, Greek nai)
etymology: From Saxon gea, yes. In the Authorized Version it does two things: it affirms (Yea, yea), and far more often it intensifies, adding a second and stronger statement to one already made — not only this, but even this.
biblical_def: Yea is chiefly an intensive. It marks the moment a sentence goes further than it had promised to go. God tells Abraham of Sarah, “I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations” (Genesis 17:16) — the blessing said once, then said again and enlarged. Proverbs uses it to climb from strength to knowledge: “A wise man is strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength” (Proverbs 24:5). Jeremiah uses it to press an indictment past what the hearer expected: prophet and priest are profane, “yea, in my house have I found their wickedness” (Jeremiah 23:11) — the corruption reaching into the temple itself. Simeon uses it to add to a mother's joy a warning she could not have wanted: “(Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,)” (Luke 2:35). As a simple affirmative the word stands in Christ's command about oaths, “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay”, where the doubling is not an oath but the plainness that makes oaths unnecessary.
webster_summary: An affirmative particle, yes; but in Scripture chiefly an intensive, adding a second and stronger clause to the first — yea, I will bless her; yea, in my house have I found their wickedness.
webster_full: YEA, adv. [Sax. gea.] Yes; a word expressing affirmation or assent.
2. It is used to enforce or intensify what has been said; not only so, but more; as, yea, and more also.
3. It is opposed to nay, as yes is to no.
4. YEA, n. An affirmative vote; as, the yeas and nays.
5. In Scripture, yea, I will bless her, Gen. 17; let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay, Matt. 5.
corruption_summary: Christ's rule that speech be simply yea or nay is broken not only by profane swearing but by the whole apparatus of emphatic assurance — I swear, honestly, to be perfectly frank — by which a man signals that his ordinary word is worth less.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord's point in Matthew 5:33-37 is not that oaths are always unlawful; He Himself answered under oath before the high priest, Paul calls God to record upon his soul, and God swears by Himself. The point is that a man whose plain word can be trusted has no need of an escalating scale of assurances. The scribes had built exactly such a scale, grading oaths by their object so that the weaker ones could be broken; Christ abolishes the scale and requires that the ordinary sentence carry full weight. Whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.

The habit worth examining is not blasphemy but padding. Every phrase a man adds to make himself believed — I promise, trust me, I really mean it — is an admission that his unadorned speech is not sufficient security, and the more such phrases he uses the less any of them will finally be worth. The remedy is not a rule about vocabulary but a reputation: say what is so, do what was said, and let the yea stand alone. The Confession permits lawful oaths where a magistrate or a solemn occasion requires them, and warns that they are not to be used lightly.
roots_summary: Hebrew has several intensives rendered yea — 'aph (also, indeed, yea), gam (also, moreover), and ken (so, thus) — while Greek uses nai for the plain affirmative.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'aph (H637) — also, yea, indeed; the commonest intensive, adding force to what precedes.
Hebrew gam (H1571) — also, moreover, even; joins a further and usually stronger clause.
Hebrew ken (H3651) — so, thus, rightly; used affirmatively of what is right or true.
Greek nai (G3483) — yea, verily, truly; the plain affirmative of Matthew 5:37.
Saxon gea — yes; the Old English affirmative that gives the English word.
usage: Of a blessing repeated and enlarged: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations (Genesis 17:16).
Of an indictment pressed further than expected: yea, in my house have I found their wickedness (Jeremiah 23:11).
Of speech that needs no oath to support it: let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Matthew 5:37).
scriptures: Genesis 17:16
And I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall be of her.
Proverbs 24:5
A wise man is strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength.
Jeremiah 23:11
For both prophet and priest are profane; yea, in my house have I found their wickedness, saith the LORD.
Matthew 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.

pos: adv. (negative and corrective; rendering Hebrew lo' and 'al, Greek ouchi)
etymology: From the Norse nei, no. Like yea it serves twice over: as the flat negative, and as a corrective that denies what was said in order to put something stronger in its place — no; rather.
biblical_def: Nay is the negative answering to yea, and Scripture uses it for two kinds of contradiction. The first is the plain denial of a falsehood, delivered without cruelty and without retreat. Sarah, afraid, denies that she laughed; the answer is three words: “Nay; but thou didst laugh” (Genesis 18:15). Eli rebukes his sons with the same word, though far too gently for the offence: “Nay, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear” (1 Samuel 2:24). Christ uses it to overturn the assumption that sudden death proves particular guilt: “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:5) — refusing the question's premise and turning it back on the questioners. The second use is Paul's, where nay denies a statement in order to replace it with a greater: after listing tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, and sword, he writes, “Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us” (Romans 8:37). Not merely survivors; more than conquerors.
webster_summary: A negative particle, no; and also a corrective, denying what was said in order to substitute something stronger — Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors.
webster_full: NAY, adv. [Norse nei.] No; a word expressing negation or refusal.
2. Not only so; but more. It is used to introduce a correction or an amplification of what precedes.
3. It is opposed to yea, as no is to yes.
4. NAY, n. A negative vote; as, the yeas and nays.
5. In Scripture, Nay; but thou didst laugh, Gen. 18; Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors, Rom. 8.
corruption_summary: The capacity to say nay plainly has been weakened by a habit of treating contradiction itself as unkind. Scripture contradicts constantly — God to Sarah, Christ to the crowd, Paul to the churches — and does so without either cruelty or hedging.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is faithful contradiction. Sarah's denial is met with Nay; but thou didst laugh, and the correction is neither softened nor pressed further than it needs to go; the LORD says the true thing once and leaves it. Christ's I tell you, Nay in Luke 13 declines to accept the premise of a question that would have let His hearers examine somebody else. A church unable to say nay loses the power to correct, and correction is one of the things love does.

Eli stands as the warning at the other end. His words to his sons were true and gentle — Nay, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear — and God's verdict on him was that he honoured his sons above the LORD and restrained them not. Saying nay is not by itself faithfulness; a rebuke that costs nothing and changes nothing is a form of neglect. The Christian standard is neither the harshness that wounds for pleasure nor the mildness that leaves sin in place, but a plainness that means what it says and acts accordingly.
roots_summary: Hebrew negates with lo' (absolute, of fact and law) and 'al (of prohibition and entreaty); Greek uses ou and its emphatic ouchi, the form behind Christ's I tell you, Nay.
roots_lines: Hebrew lo' (H3808) — not, no; the absolute negative of fact and of the Decalogue.
Hebrew 'al (H408) — not; the negative of entreaty and prohibition, softer than lo'.
Greek ouchi (G3780) — nay, not so; the emphatic negative of Luke 13:5.
Greek hupernikao (G5245) — to be more than conqueror, to vanquish beyond; Paul's word in Romans 8:37.
Norse nei — no; the root of the English particle, distinct from the Saxon na.
usage: Of a falsehood plainly contradicted: Nay; but thou didst laugh (Genesis 18:15).
Of a premise refused and turned back on the questioner: I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent (Luke 13:5).
Of a denial that substitutes something greater: Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors (Romans 8:37).
scriptures: Genesis 18:15
Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh.
1 Samuel 2:24
Nay, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear: ye make the LORD'S people to transgress.
Luke 13:5
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
Romans 8:37
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.

pos: conj. (of negative purpose; rendering Hebrew pen, Greek me pos and hina me)
etymology: From Saxon þy læs þe, by the less that — worn down to lest. It introduces the thing to be avoided, and so is the particle of every warning in Scripture: the danger named so that it may be escaped.
biblical_def: Lest introduces what must not happen, and it is therefore the grammar of warning. It appears in Eve's report of the prohibition — “neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die” (Genesis 3:3) — and in Moses' charge against the peculiar danger of prosperity: “Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 6:12). That warning is given precisely at the point where Israel is promised great and goodly cities she did not build; comfort, not hardship, is the setting for forgetting God. Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches with the same particle governing both halves: “Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain” (Proverbs 30:9). Christ commands watchfulness in Gethsemane with it: “Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38). And Paul uses it for the danger of discipline pressed too far, urging the Corinthians to forgive a repentant offender “lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2 Corinthians 2:7).
webster_summary: A conjunction introducing what is to be prevented or avoided; that not, for fear that. In Scripture it is the particle of warning — beware lest thou forget, watch and pray lest ye enter into temptation.
webster_full: LEST, conj. [Sax. þy læs þe, by the less that.] That not; for fear that.
2. It introduces a clause expressing something to be prevented; as, take heed lest ye fall.
3. It governs the subjunctive mood, the event being contingent and undesired.
4. It answers to the Hebrew pen and the Greek me pos.
5. In Scripture, beware lest thou forget the LORD, Deut. 6; Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation, Mark 14.
corruption_summary: Warning has fallen out of favour as a mode of Christian address, treated as fear-mongering or as inconsistent with assurance. Scripture warns constantly, and warns the saints most of all; the warnings are among the means by which God keeps His people.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection runs that if the elect cannot finally fall away, warnings to them are empty threats. The Reformed answer is that God ordains means as well as ends, and the warnings are among the means. Hebrews is addressed to professing Christians and is full of lest: lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief. These are not idle. The believer who reads them and takes heed is being kept by them, and the man who dismisses them as inapplicable to himself has already shown the disposition they were written against.

Deuteronomy 6:12 identifies the direction from which the danger usually comes, and it is not persecution. Israel is warned about forgetting God at the exact moment she is given houses full of good things she did not fill. Prosperity is the more dangerous climate because nothing in it announces itself as a trial. Agur's prayer is the wise man's response — asking to be spared both extremities, since riches tempt to denial and want tempts to theft. A church in comfortable circumstances that has stopped hearing warnings is in the precise condition Moses feared.
roots_summary: Hebrew pen introduces the undesired contingency; Greek uses me pos and hina me with the subjunctive. The particle always governs an event to be avoided, never one intended.
roots_lines: Hebrew pen (H6435) — lest, that not, peradventure; the standard particle of negative purpose.
Greek hina me (G2443, G3361) — that not, lest; purpose clause with the negative.
Greek me pos (G3381) — lest by any means, lest perhaps; used where the danger is uncertain but real.
Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget; the specific danger of Deuteronomy 6:12.
Greek peirasmos (G3986) — temptation, trial, testing; what the disciples were to watch and pray against.
usage: Of the danger attending prosperity: beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt (Deuteronomy 6:12).
Of both riches and poverty as temptations: Lest I be full, and deny thee... or lest I be poor, and steal (Proverbs 30:9).
Of watchfulness commanded in the garden: Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation (Mark 14:38).
scriptures: Genesis 3:3
But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die.
Deuteronomy 6:12
Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.
Proverbs 30:9
Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.
Mark 14:38
Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak.

pos: prep. and conj. of time (rendering Hebrew 'ad, Greek heos); distinguish the verb till, to cultivate
etymology: From Saxon til, to or unto, a preposition of limit. It marks the boundary of a duration — the point up to which something continues. The verb to till, meaning to cultivate the ground, is a wholly separate word, and the Authorized Version uses both.
biblical_def: Till marks the end of a duration: the point at which a state ceases. Its most solemn use fixes the entrance of sin into a creature made without it: “Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee” (Ezekiel 28:15). Everything before that word was good; everything after is ruin, and the single conjunction carries the whole fall. It also marks patient forbearance. The dresser of the vineyard pleads for the barren fig tree: “let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it” (Luke 13:8) — a reprieve with a limit and a labour attached to it. The Song uses it to forbid the forcing of love: “that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please” (Song of Solomon 2:7), thrice repeated in the book, a charge against haste in the one matter where haste is most tempting. And Christ uses it to govern the conduct of His messengers in a strange city: “there abide till ye go thence” (Matthew 10:11). The word to distinguish from all these is the verb of Genesis 3:23, “to till the ground”.
webster_summary: A preposition and conjunction of time, marking the limit up to which something continues; until. Distinguish the verb to till, to cultivate. In Scripture it fixes the entrance of iniquity into a perfect creature and the term of God's forbearance.
webster_full: TILL, prep. [Sax. til, to.] To the time of; until; as, wait till morning.
2. As a conjunction, to the time when; as, abide till I come.
3. TILL, v.t. [Sax. tilian, to labor.] To cultivate; to prepare and use for the production of crops. A wholly distinct word.
4. TILL, n. A money drawer in a shop or counter.
5. In Scripture, till iniquity was found in thee, Ezek. 28; till I shall dig about it, and dung it, Luke 13.
corruption_summary: God's forbearance is regularly mistaken for indifference or for permanence. Scripture's till keeps a term on it: the fig tree is spared this year also, the vinedresser digs and dungs, and then the matter is settled one way or the other.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable in Luke 13 is unusually exact about mercy. The tree has had three years and produced nothing; the owner's judgment is entirely just; and the dresser asks not for indefinite reprieve but for one more season with work done to it. Peter explains the same principle at the level of history: the Lord is not slack concerning His promise but is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish. Delay is mercy, not slackness, and it is not endless. To read God's patience as evidence that judgment will not come is the reasoning of the scoffers Peter describes.

Ezekiel 28:15 supplies the other half. The creature described was perfect in his ways from the day of his creation — a statement no one could have inferred, and one that forecloses any doctrine making evil eternal or making God its author. Iniquity was found in him; it had a beginning within a will that had been made good. This is the ground of the Confession's careful statement that God is not the author of sin, and that the creature's fall proceeded from himself. Between that till and the till of the fig tree stands the whole history of God's dealing with rebels.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ad is the preposition of limit, up to and including; Greek uses heos with the same force. The verb till renders Hebrew 'abad, to serve or work the ground, an unrelated root.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ad (H5704) — as far as, up to, until; the preposition of temporal and spatial limit.
Greek heos (G2193) — until, as far as; the ordinary conjunction of duration in the New Testament.
Hebrew 'avlah (H5766) — iniquity, unrighteousness; what was found in the creature of Ezekiel 28:15.
Hebrew 'abad (H5647) — to work, serve, till the ground; the root behind the unrelated verb to till.
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patience; the disposition behind every scriptural reprieve.
usage: Of the moment sin entered a creature made perfect: till iniquity was found in thee (Ezekiel 28:15).
Of a reprieve granted with a term and a labour attached: let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it (Luke 13:8).
Of love not to be forced or hurried: that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please (Song of Solomon 2:7).
scriptures: Ezekiel 28:15
Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee.
Luke 13:8
And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it:
Song of Solomon 2:7
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
Genesis 3:23
Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.

pos: adv. (of addition; rendering Hebrew gam and the waw-consecutive, Greek de and eti)
etymology: A compound of more and over — over and above what has been said. It adds a further item to a discourse already in progress, and in the prophets it commonly opens a fresh word from the LORD in an unbroken series.
biblical_def: Moreover adds. It is the hinge on which a speech or a narrative turns to its next item without changing subject, and its steady recurrence in the prophets is itself instructive: God's word comes not as a single utterance but as a sustained address. “Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears” (Ezekiel 3:10) — the prophet is commissioned in stages, and this stage concerns not what he will say but how he must first receive. Zechariah's interpreting angel uses it to press an explanation further: “He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth” (Zechariah 5:6). Chronicles uses it to continue the record of a reign: “Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah” (2 Chronicles 27:4). And in ordinary conversation it does exactly what it does today, adding a detail to hospitality already offered: “She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in” (Genesis 24:25).
webster_summary: An adverb of addition: beyond what has been said, further, besides. In Scripture it commonly introduces the next stage of a continuing discourse, and in the prophets a further word from the LORD in an unbroken series.
webster_full: MOREOVER, adv. [more and over.] Beyond what has been said; further; besides; also.
2. It connects a new particular to a discourse already begun, without changing the subject.
3. It answers to the Hebrew gam and to the Greek de and eti.
4. Furthermore and besides are of the same class of connectives.
5. In Scripture, Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, Ezek. 3; She said moreover unto him, Gen. 24.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's commission puts receiving before speaking — the word taken into the heart and heard with the ears before it is delivered. The order is regularly reversed by men who study Scripture only for what they will say of it to others.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that the messenger must first be a hearer. Ezekiel is told to receive all God's words in his heart and hear them with his ears, and only then to go to the captives and speak. The same order governs Ezra, who prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and afterward to teach in Israel statutes and judgments — seek, do, teach, in that sequence. A preacher who reverses it becomes an intermediary handling material he has never let touch him.

The danger is not confined to the pulpit. Any Christian who reads chiefly to have something to contribute — in a class, in an argument, on a screen — is exposed to it. The remedy is a habit of reading in which nothing is passed on for a time, and the first question asked of every text is what it requires of the reader himself. Ezekiel's ministry was largely unsuccessful by any visible measure, and the LORD told him beforehand that it would be; what was required of him was faithfulness in receiving and delivering, and that is what was commended.
roots_summary: Hebrew adds with gam (also, moreover) and with the ordinary narrative waw; Greek uses de (and, but, moreover) and eti (yet, still, further). The English compound simply joins more to over.
roots_lines: Hebrew gam (H1571) — also, moreover, yea; the commonest additive particle.
Hebrew waw-consecutive — the narrative connective that carries a story or a discourse forward step by step.
Greek de (G1161) — and, but, moreover; a light connective marking the next item.
Greek eti (G2089) — yet, still, further; adds something beyond what was said.
Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, hearken, obey; what Ezekiel was to do before speaking.
usage: Of a prophet commissioned first to receive: Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words... receive in thine heart (Ezekiel 3:10).
Of an explanation pressed further: He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth (Zechariah 5:6).
Of hospitality offered with an added detail: She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough (Genesis 24:25).
scriptures: Ezekiel 3:10
Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears.
Zechariah 5:6
And I said, What is it? And he said, This is an ephah that goeth forth. He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth.
2 Chronicles 27:4
Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests he built castles and towers.
Genesis 24:25
She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in.

pos: adv. (of place, time, and inference; rendering Hebrew mizzeh, Greek enteuthen and hupage)
etymology: From Saxon heonan, from here. It is one of a set of three — hence from this place, thence from that place, whence from what place — which English has now largely surrendered to the single word where from. The Authorized Version keeps all three exactly.
biblical_def: Hence means from this place, and its most memorable use is a command of departure spoken to Satan: “Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Matthew 4:10). The dismissal ends the third temptation, and it is issued with Scripture — the same weapon used in each of the three exchanges. The word is also the vehicle of one of the great acts of faith in Genesis: Joseph, dying in Egypt at the height of his power, takes an oath of his brethren, “God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence” (Genesis 50:25). He believed the promise of a land he would not see again, and Hebrews names this dying charge as the instance of his faith. Elijah is sent away from the coming drought with the same word — “Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith” (1 Kings 17:3) — and the Pharisees use it to move Christ along with a report about Herod (Luke 13:31).
webster_summary: An adverb meaning from this place, and by extension from this time or from this cause. In Scripture it dismisses the tempter — Get thee hence, Satan — and carries Joseph's dying charge that his bones be carried up out of Egypt.
webster_full: HENCE, adv. [Sax. heonan.] From this place; away; as, go hence.
2. From this time; in the future; as, a week hence.
3. From this cause or reason; therefore; as, hence it follows.
4. It is one of a set with thence, from that place, and whence, from what place.
5. In Scripture, Get thee hence, Satan, Matt. 4; ye shall carry up my bones from hence, Gen. 50.
corruption_summary: The temptation narrative is widely treated as symbolic drama rather than a real encounter with a real adversary. Christ answers a person, dismisses a person, and does so by quoting Scripture — which is also the pattern left for His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern theology has been embarrassed by the devil, and the embarrassment produces two errors. The first demythologises him into a symbol of the human capacity for evil, which leaves the wilderness account as an interior monologue and makes the second commandment of the exchange — Get thee hence — unintelligible. The second inflates him into an almost equal power, so that the Christian life becomes a war between comparable forces. Scripture holds neither. Satan is a real creature, entirely subject to God, defeated at the cross, and to be resisted steadfast in the faith.

The manner of Christ's resistance is the part most worth imitating and the part most often skipped. He does not argue, negotiate, or reason from His own authority; three times He answers It is written, and each citation comes from Deuteronomy. The command to depart is issued only after the third assault and is grounded in the text He quotes. A believer who has no Scripture in him has nothing to say in the same situation, which is one plain reason why the memorising of Scripture is not an optional refinement of the Christian life.
roots_summary: Hebrew mizzeh means from this; Greek enteuthen is from here, while hupage is the imperative go. The Saxon set heonan, þanon, hwanon gives English hence, thence, whence.
roots_lines: Hebrew mizzeh (H2088) — from this, from hence; the preposition min with the demonstrative.
Greek enteuthen (G1782) — from this place, hence; used of departure and of source.
Greek hupago (G5217) — to go away, depart; the imperative in Get thee hence, Satan.
Hebrew 'etsem (H6106) — a bone; what Joseph charged his brethren to carry up out of Egypt.
Saxon heonan — from here; the Old English adverb, one of the set with thence and whence.
usage: Of the tempter dismissed by Scripture: Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written (Matthew 4:10).
Of faith in a promise the dying man will not see kept: ye shall carry up my bones from hence (Genesis 50:25).
Of a prophet sent away before a judgment falls: Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward (1 Kings 17:3).
scriptures: Matthew 4:10
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
Genesis 50:25
And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.
1 Kings 17:3
Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan.
Luke 13:31
The same day there came certain of the Pharisees, saying unto him, Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee.

etymology: From Saxon betweox, related to two — the space or relation between two parties. The Authorized Version uses it interchangeably with between, and it clusters remarkably in Genesis, where it is the word of covenants made between men and witnessed by God.
biblical_def: Betwixt is simply between, but in the Authorized Version it falls almost entirely in the patriarchal narratives, where it becomes the preposition of covenant. Circumcision is given as “a token of the covenant betwixt me and you” (Genesis 17:11) — a sign cut into the body of every male, marking a bond that a man carries whether he thinks of it or not. When Jacob and Laban part after twenty years of mutual suspicion, they raise a heap of stones and swear over it, and the word recurs four times in a single chapter: “God is witness betwixt me and thee” (Genesis 31:50), “this heap, and behold this pillar, which I have cast betwixt me and thee” (Genesis 31:51), “The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor... judge betwixt us” (Genesis 31:53). Two men who do not trust each other invoke God as the third party to their treaty, which is what an oath is for. Ephron uses it more lightly, waving away the price of a burial field: “what is that betwixt me and thee?” (Genesis 23:15).
webster_summary: A preposition meaning between — in the space or the relation dividing two parties. In Scripture it is the word of covenant: the token betwixt God and Abraham, and the heap of witness betwixt Jacob and Laban.
webster_full: BETWIXT, prep. [Sax. betweox, from twa, two.] Between; in the intermediate space.
2. From one to another, noting passage or relation; as, a covenant betwixt them.
3. It is used of two parties only; among is used of more than two.
4. It is now less common than between, and belongs chiefly to the older and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, a token of the covenant betwixt me and you, Gen. 17; God is witness betwixt me and thee, Gen. 31.
corruption_summary: Covenant has been reduced to contract — an agreement between parties for mutual advantage, dissolvable when the advantage ends. Scripture's covenants are sworn before God, sealed with a sign, and binding whether or not they remain convenient.
corruption_paragraphs: The difference shows most plainly in marriage. A contract is an exchange of considerations and ends when one party defaults or when both prefer to stop; a covenant is a bond made before God, who is named as witness and judge. Malachi says exactly this — the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy covenant — and it is the ground on which he condemns the treachery of divorce. The modern reduction of marriage to a terminable arrangement between consenting adults is not a development of the biblical idea but its replacement.

Genesis 31 shows the machinery of a covenant plainly, and it is worth noticing what is present: two parties who have every reason to distrust each other, a physical sign that will outlast the conversation, an oath naming God as judge, and a meal eaten together. The circumcision covenant of Genesis 17 has the same elements at a higher level, with God Himself as one of the parties and the sign cut into the flesh. Where covenant is understood, obligation does not depend on continuing goodwill; where it is not, nothing does.
roots_summary: Hebrew ben, between, is often repeated before each party (between me and between thee), an idiom the translators smooth into a single preposition; Greek uses metaxu. The Saxon root is twa, two.
roots_lines: Hebrew ben (H996) — between, among; regularly repeated before each party in a covenant formula.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, treaty, or alliance; the bond made betwixt the parties.
Hebrew 'oth (H226) — a sign or token; circumcision as the mark of the Abrahamic covenant.
Hebrew 'ed (H5707) — a witness; God invoked as the third party at Mizpah.
Greek metaxu (G3342) — between, in the midst; the New Testament preposition of the same sense.
usage: Of the sign of the Abrahamic covenant: a token of the covenant betwixt me and you (Genesis 17:11).
Of God invoked as witness between two suspicious parties: God is witness betwixt me and thee (Genesis 31:50).
Of a price waved away in courtesy: what is that betwixt me and thee? (Genesis 23:15).
scriptures: Genesis 17:11
And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
Genesis 31:50
If thou shalt afflict my daughters, or if thou shalt take other wives beside my daughters, no man is with us; see, God is witness betwixt me and thee.
Genesis 31:53
The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.
Genesis 23:15
My lord, hearken unto me: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver; what is that betwixt me and thee? bury therefore thy dead.

pos: adv. (often, frequently; rendering Hebrew kammah and Greek posakis and pukna)
etymology: From Saxon oft, the older and shorter form of often. The Authorized Version keeps both, and also the compound ofttimes. Its characteristic construction is the exclamation or question of frequency: how oft.
biblical_def: Oft is often, and its most important uses are questions and exclamations about how many times a thing happens. Peter asks the question that every wronged man asks: “Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). He supposes himself generous, since the rabbis allowed three; the Lord's answer of seventy times seven abolishes the counting altogether, and the parable that follows explains why — a servant forgiven ten thousand talents has no standing to number a hundred pence. The psalmist uses the same form to marvel at Israel's persistence in provoking God: “How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness, and grieve him in the desert!” (Psalm 78:40). Job uses it to challenge the tidy doctrine of his friends, asking how often the candle of the wicked is really put out (Job 21:17). And it marks the ceremonial precision of the Pharisees, who “except they wash their hands oft, eat not, holding the tradition of the elders” (Mark 7:3).
webster_summary: An adverb meaning often or frequently; the older and shorter form. In Scripture it appears chiefly in the question or exclamation of frequency — how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?
webster_full: OFT, adv. [Sax. oft.] Often; frequently; not rarely.
2. It is the shorter and older form of often, and is now chiefly poetic or scriptural.
3. OFTTIMES, adv. Frequently; often; many times.
4. How oft is an interrogative or exclamatory phrase of frequency.
5. In Scripture, how oft shall my brother sin against me? Matt. 18; How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness, Psa. 78.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is now commonly presented as a therapeutic act performed for the sake of the one forgiving — releasing oneself from bitterness. Scripture grounds it elsewhere: in the immeasurable debt God has remitted, which makes the counting of offences against us absurd.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-help account of forgiveness is not wholly false — bitterness does corrode — but as the primary ground it fails at exactly the point where forgiveness is hard. If I forgive for my own peace, then when forgiving costs more peace than it gives I have no reason left. Christ's ground is different and does not shift: the servant is forgiven ten thousand talents, an unpayable sum, and then seizes a fellow servant for a hundred pence. The parable ends severely, and the severity is the point — an unforgiving spirit in one who claims to be forgiven calls the claim itself into question.

Peter's question also exposes the instinct to quantify. How oft? assumes a ledger, and the Lord's answer — seventy times seven — is not a higher number but the end of numbering. This does not abolish justice; Scripture provides for rebuke, for restitution, for church discipline, and for the magistrate's sword, and forgiving a brother is not the same as pretending nothing happened. But it does forbid the running account. What Christ requires is a disposition, not an allowance that eventually runs out.
roots_summary: Hebrew asks frequency with kammah, how much or how many; Greek uses posakis (how often) and pukna (frequently). The Saxon oft is the parent of English often.
roots_lines: Hebrew kammah (H4100) — how much, how many, how often; the interrogative of quantity and frequency.
Greek posakis (G4212) — how often, how many times; Peter's word in Matthew 18:21.
Greek pukna (G4437) — often, frequently; used of the Pharisees' repeated washings.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, remit, forgive; the verb governed by Peter's question.
Hebrew marah (H4784) — to be rebellious, to provoke; Israel's repeated act in Psalm 78:40.
usage: Of forgiveness that refuses to be counted: Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? (Matthew 18:21).
Of astonishment at persistent provocation: How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness (Psalm 78:40).
Of ceremonial washing kept as tradition: except they wash their hands oft, eat not (Mark 7:3).
scriptures: Matthew 18:21
Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?
Psalm 78:40
How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness, and grieve him in the desert!
How oft is the candle of the wicked put out! and how oft cometh their destruction upon them! God distributeth sorrows in his anger.
Mark 7:3
For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, except they wash their hands oft, eat not, holding the tradition of the elders.

pos: adv. and adj. (grievously, severely; rendering Hebrew me'od and gadol, Greek sphodra)
etymology: From Saxon sar, painful or grievous. In the Authorized Version it is chiefly an adverb of degree meaning grievously or severely — not the modern noun for a wound. Sore afraid, sore vexed, and sore broken are its standing phrases.
biblical_def: Sore in the Authorized Version usually means grievously or severely, an adverb of degree rather than the modern noun. Its commonest phrase is sore afraid: Abimelech, warned in a dream that he has taken another man's wife, tells his servants, and “the men were sore afraid” (Genesis 20:8). It measures the weight of God's hand in chastening: “For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore” (Psalm 38:2), where David does not soften the description of a discipline he acknowledges to be deserved. It measures the guilt of a king: Ahaz “made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the LORD” (2 Chronicles 28:19). And Ecclesiastes uses it as an adjective for an evil observed under the sun: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt” (Ecclesiastes 5:13) — wealth hoarded until it damages the man who holds it, which the Preacher classes among the grievous things.
webster_summary: An adverb and adjective meaning grievously, severely, or painful. In Scripture chiefly adverbial — sore afraid, presseth me sore, transgressed sore — measuring the degree of fear, of chastening, or of guilt.
webster_full: SORE, a. [Sax. sar.] Painful; tender to the touch; as, a sore wound.
2. Grievous; severe; violent; as, a sore famine, a sore evil.
3. SORE, adv. Greatly; violently; severely; as, sore afraid, sore vexed.
4. SORE, n. A place in an animal body where the skin and flesh are bruised or broken.
5. In Scripture, the men were sore afraid, Gen. 20; thy hand presseth me sore, Psa. 38.
corruption_summary: The Preacher's sore evil — riches kept by their owners to their own hurt — is not a warning against wealth but against hoarding, and it names the damage as falling first on the man who hoards.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes is not teaching that property is wrong. Scripture establishes and protects it, commends diligence, and honours the man who leaves an inheritance to his children's children. What the Preacher observes is a particular ruin: wealth held, watched, and never used, until the holding itself becomes the injury — sleeplessness, suspicion, and finally a loss in which nothing remains for the son. The rich fool of Luke 12 is the same man in a parable, pulling down barns to build greater ones on the night his soul is required of him.

The biblical remedy is not asceticism but liberality. Paul's charge to the rich is exact and worth stating in full: that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate. Notice that enjoyment is commanded as well as giving. Between the ascetic who despises God's gifts and the miser who cannot release them stands the steward, who both uses and distributes what was never finally his.
roots_summary: Hebrew intensifies with me'od (very, exceedingly) and gadol (great); the phrase yare' me'od gives sore afraid. Greek uses sphodra, exceedingly. The Saxon sar means painful or grievous.
roots_lines: Hebrew me'od (H3966) — very, exceedingly, greatly; the standard intensive rendered sore.
Hebrew yare' (H3372) — to fear, to be afraid; with me'od it gives the phrase sore afraid.
Hebrew ra'ah cholah (H7451, H2470) — a sick or grievous evil; the sore evil of Ecclesiastes 5:13.
Greek sphodra (G4970) — exceedingly, greatly; the New Testament intensive of the same force.
Saxon sar — painful, grievous; the root of both the adverb and the modern noun.
usage: Of great fear at a divine warning: and the men were sore afraid (Genesis 20:8).
Of chastening acknowledged as heavy and deserved: thy hand presseth me sore (Psalm 38:2).
Of wealth hoarded to the owner's hurt: There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun (Ecclesiastes 5:13).
scriptures: Genesis 20:8
Therefore Abimelech rose early in the morning, and called all his servants, and told all these things in their ears: and the men were sore afraid.
Psalm 38:2
For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore.
2 Chronicles 28:19
For the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel; for he made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the LORD.
Ecclesiastes 5:13
There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt.

pos: pron. and adj. (universal relative of things; rendering Hebrew kol 'asher, Greek pas hos and ho ean)
etymology: A compound of what, so, and ever, the counterpart of whosoever: that one universalises persons, this one things. It leaves the thing unnamed and the class unbounded — whatever it may be, of whatever kind.
biblical_def: Whatsoever is the universal relative of things, and Scripture uses it to draw boundaries around the whole of life rather than a part of it. Paul makes it the rule of Christian conduct without remainder: “And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him” (Colossians 3:17). There is no category of neutral action left over. He uses it again to fix the mind's diet: “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report” (Philippians 4:8) — six times, so that the standard cannot be narrowed to one field. And he makes it the test of a doubtful conscience: “whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Romans 14:23), a sentence that settles a great many disputed questions by referring them to the believer's own assurance before God. Set against these stands the anarchy Moses forbids, where the word describes a nation with no standard but preference: “every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes” (Deuteronomy 12:8).
webster_summary: The universal relative of things; whatever, of whatever kind, without exception. In Scripture it governs the whole of conduct — whatsoever ye do — the whole of thought, and the conscience: whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
webster_full: WHATSOEVER, pron. [what, so and ever.] Whatever; being this or that; of whatever kind.
2. It is a compound relative, including both the antecedent and the relative.
3. It is emphatic, and excludes every exception of kind, degree or circumstance.
4. Whosoever is the corresponding form of persons; wheresoever of place; whensoever of time.
5. In Scripture, whatsoever ye do in word or deed, Col. 3; whatsoever is not of faith is sin, Rom. 14.
corruption_summary: The division of life into sacred and secular spheres — some acts done before God, most done in a neutral zone — is abolished by this word. Whatsoever ye do leaves nothing outside the reach of Christ's lordship.
corruption_paragraphs: The two-storey model of the Christian life is widespread and comfortable: prayer, worship, and giving belong to God, while work, leisure, money, and appetite are governed by ordinary prudence. Colossians 3:17 dismantles it in a sentence. Every word and every deed is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus and with thanksgiving, which means that the eating of a meal and the doing of a day's work are as much acts of worship as the singing of a psalm. The Reformers recovered exactly this against a scheme that had graded life by proximity to the altar, and the Puritans built a whole practical divinity on it.

Deuteronomy 12:8 supplies the alternative, and it is the description of a society, not merely of an individual: every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes. The book of Judges ends by repeating it as the epitaph of an era. The modern insistence that each person determine his own truth and his own good is not a novelty but the oldest arrangement in the record, and its results are catalogued in the last five chapters of Judges. Against it Paul sets a standard given from outside — things true, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report — none of which is measured by the observer's preference.
roots_summary: Hebrew builds the universal of things with kol (all, every) and the relative 'asher; Greek uses pas hos or ho ean with the subjunctive. The English compound joins what, so, and ever.
roots_lines: Hebrew kol 'asher (H3605, H834) — all that, whatsoever; the standard universal of things.
Greek ho ean (G3739, G1437) — whatsoever; the relative with the particle of contingency and the subjunctive.
Greek pas (G3956) — all, every; with the relative it excludes every exception.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to consider, to think on; the command attached to Philippians 4:8.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, conviction; the standard by which a doubtful action is judged in Romans 14:23.
usage: Of the whole of conduct brought under one rule: whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus (Colossians 3:17).
Of the standard set for the mind: whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest (Philippians 4:8).
Of a people with no standard but preference: every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes (Deuteronomy 12:8).
scriptures: Colossians 3:17
And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
Philippians 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Romans 14:23
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Deuteronomy 12:8
Ye shall not do after all the things that we do here this day, every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes.
